common_name: TropicSnow Peach (University of Florida Low-Chill White Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant, in full sun with excellent drainage; TropicSnow needs only about 150-200 chilling hours, among the lowest chill requirements of any named peach, making it reliable even in mild Gulf Coast winters.

directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun with excellent drainage, and prune to an open-vase shape in the early years to let light into the canopy. TropicSnow was released by the University of Florida breeding program as one of the lowest-chill white-fleshed peaches available, developed to give far-southern and even subtropical growers a genuine tree-ripened peach where standard varieties fail to bloom reliably. The medium-sized freestone fruit has creamy white skin blushed with red and sweet, low-acid white flesh, a flavor profile many gardeners prefer to the tangier yellow-fleshed low-chill peaches bred for the same region. Thin fruit to 6-8 inches apart when marble-sized to improve size and quality, and expect an early harvest, typically in late spring, well ahead of summer heat.

common_name: Flordacrest Peach (University of Florida Low-Chill Freestone Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant, in full sun with excellent drainage; Flordacrest needs roughly 300 chilling hours, low enough for reliable bloom and fruit set across most of the Gulf South.

directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun with excellent drainage, since peach roots are quickly damaged by standing water. Flordacrest is a low-chill freestone peach from the University of Florida breeding program, bred to extend the low-chill peach harvest window with medium to large fruit, attractive red-blushed yellow skin, and firm, good-flavored yellow flesh that holds up well for fresh eating. It is self-fertile and does not require a second tree for pollination, though planting a second early-blooming low-chill peach nearby can improve fruit set in a light bloom year. Thin fruit clusters to 6-8 inches apart when fruit reaches marble size to improve final size, and expect ripening in late spring to early summer, consistent with other low-chill Florida-bred peaches.
